title: VR Live Events
desc: Plan and run a live virtual-reality or virtual event: platforms, access, moderation, safety and measures of success.
outcomes: Prepare tech checks and run sheets.
task: Plan and run a 30-minute virtual event for 10 to 20 people, with rehearsal, moderation, accessibility, feedback and report.
condition: Computers or VR headsets as available, a free event platform, two peers and a mentor.
standard: Rehearsal passes; moderation rules enforced; accessibility options present; feedback from 80% of attendees; report with data; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Event planners, teachers, community groups, trainers.
evidence: plan, run sheet, tech checklist, feedback report
modules: A virtual event can run on a flat screen, a headset or both. Pick the format that your audience can use.

Headsets give presence but need equipment and comfort checks.
Hybrid events stream a live room to virtual guests.

ladder: Event formats and platforms

L1: learner can name formats. Focus module: Event formats and platforms (Understand, 3 h). A virtual event can run on a flat screen, a headset or both. Pick the format that your audience can use. Key points: Desktop 3D spaces and video rooms are easiest to join. Headsets give presence but need equipment and comfort checks. Hybrid events stream a live room to virtual guests. Capacity, bandwidth and cost vary.

Teach: open with the worked example. A training session uses a desktop 3D room so that every learner can join from a laptop, while a product launch offers a headset option for early adopters. Then set the activity: Compare three formats for one event goal. Mark against the standard: Table includes device needs and access. Check at this level: Name a format. Model answer: Desktop 3D, headset VR or hybrid.
Goals and audience

L2: learner knows safety. Focus module: Goals and audience (Create, 3 h). Define what success looks like before choosing tools. Key points: Write one goal with a number, such as 80 attendees and 70 per cent stay to the end. Know the devices and bandwidth of the audience. Plan for time zones and languages. Set a budget.

Teach: open with the worked example. A community group aims for 60 attendees with 4 out of 5 satisfaction and chooses a desktop space after a survey shows only 5 per cent own headsets. Then set the activity: Write goals for your pilot event. Mark against the standard: Goals are measurable. Check at this level: Why a fallback? Model answer: Protect the session.
Technical checks

L3: learner can check tech. Focus module: Technical checks (Apply, 4 h). Test everything on real devices before show time. Key points: Accounts, links, audio, avatars and backups. Test on each device type and connection. Helper desk and a backup video link. Record known issues.

Teach: open with the worked example. A fallback video link saves a session when the 3D room fails to load for ten attendees. Then set the activity: Make a ten-item checklist and test. Mark against the standard: Checklist is tested on three devices. Check at this level: Code of conduct use? Model answer: Set behaviour rules.
Moderation and safety

L4: learner can run a session. Focus module: Moderation and safety (Evaluate, 4 h). Virtual spaces need clear rules and active moderation. Key points: Code of conduct; tools to mute, block and report. Age rules and parental consent; no personal data sharing. Trained moderators and escalation steps. Record incidents.

Teach: open with the worked example. A disruptive participant is muted, removed and reported according to the code. Then set the activity: Write rules and an escalation plan. Mark against the standard: Clear and tested. Check at this level: Motion sickness fix? Model answer: Teleport movement or breaks.
Accessibility and comfort

L5: learner can analyse. Focus module: Accessibility and comfort (Evaluate, 4 h). Everyone should be able to take part. Key points: Captions, transcripts and keyboard options. Motion-sickness settings such as teleport movement and breaks. Time zones, breaks and short sessions. Alternatives for those without headsets.

Teach: open with the worked example. Teleport movement and 10-minute breaks reduce discomfort for headset users. Then set the activity: Write an access plan. Mark against the standard: Measures listed. Check at this level: Time zone issue? Model answer: Choose fair times.
Live run
L6: learner can lead. Focus module: Live run (Create, 4 h). Deliver your pilot event. Key points: Welcome, rules, content, Q&A and close. Handle problems calmly. Collect feedback. Record attendance.

Teach: open with the worked example. The pilot finishes on time with 14 attendees and 3 technical issues, all solved. Then set the activity: Run the pilot. Mark against the standard: Mentor observes. Check at this level: Metric? Model answer: Attendance or rating.
Measure and report

L7: learner can audit. Focus module: Measure and report (Analyse, 3 h). Learn from the data. Key points: Attendance, time in event and feedback scores. Fix top issues. Share results. Plan the next event.

Teach: open with the worked example. Average rating 4.3 and 80 per cent stayed to the end. Then set the activity: Write a report. Mark against the standard: Numbers real. Check at this level: Roles? Model answer: Host, tech, moderator.
